entries.title: AI Slop Is Ruining Cute Animals on the Internet
entries.summary: Pet owners, rescue agencies, and wildlife groups are calling for new safeguards as AI makes it harder to tell whether animals, from polar bears to house cats, are real or fake.
entries.content:
AI-generated videos and pictures are destroying one of the largest and most enduring sources of joy and compassion on the internet: animals. Whether the imagery features sailors rescuing a polar bear, baby cows separated from their mothers, or a lost pet that was miraculously found, many people have reached the point where they can’t take the creatures on their feeds at face value anymore. The explosion of deepfakes and AI slop over the past few years has led to widespread frustration among viewers, creators, and organizations that support animals, forcing everyone to hunt in the pixels for glitches or other telltale signs of AI.

Mibbby Butler was overjoyed one day in April when she received a text message that her lost cat, Brooklyn, had supposedly been found. Her roommate’s boyfriend had allegedly taken the cat and dumped him 30 minutes away in the Los Angeles suburbs the day prior. Butler quickly posted a missing poster on social media, and she was driving around with her roommate searching for Brooklyn when a stranger sent her a photo. In it, he is sitting on a kitchen counter while being embraced by a girl.

“My baby is OK!” Butler exclaimed to her roommate. But if she wanted to get him back, the person said, she would have to pay money up front for Brooklyn’s purported temporary care. That’s when Butler sensed she was being scammed and began looking closer at the photo.

Brooklyn was posing the same way as he had in the picture Butler used for the missing poster. In both images, a Torani syrup bottle and a microwave can be seen in the background, except in the new photo, the label text was garbled, a classic sign that it was AI-generated. A disheartened Butler didn’t pay up. “I didn’t know people scammed for lost pets,” she says, noting she also didn’t report the incident to police because she wasn’t sure a crime had occurred. Four months later, Brooklyn is still missing.

The flood of fakes has been no easier on the creators of authentic content. The nonprofit We Animals has published the work of 175 photojournalists who have documented alleged animal abuse and other harms at farms, circuses, and scientific labs. The material can be shocking, which naturally invites skepticism, says Eva von Jagow, the group’s marketing manager. For instance, drone footage We Animals shared of rows and rows of hutches allegedly used to shelter calves separated from their moms on a dairy farm in Arizona looks almost too mesmerizingly perfect to be real.

In the past, people have claimed We Animals’ work is staged or photoshopped. It’s no surprise, then, that some viewers have begun accusing the group of relying on AI, even though it bans the photographers it works with from using the technology. “How to prove it's not AI?” an Instagram user commented earlier this month on the dairy farm video.

To convince audiences that its content is authentic, We Animals expects it will have to start sharing behind-the-scenes clips and more details about the steps staffers take to verify submissions. It also plans to adopt technology that embeds the provenance and editing history of photographs and videos into digital files. Victoria de Martigny, the group’s director of visual content, says preserving trust is crucial, or else it could “open up the door to people questioning all of the work,” and “we don’t ever want to be in that position.”

Real, evocative images often pull on viewers’ heartstrings and are an important way for conservation and welfare projects to attract donations. But for the owners of AI slop accounts, synthetic imagery can be a convenient path to collecting likes and ad revenue. Since fakes are much cheaper to produce, they appear to be drowning out real clips in social feeds and search results, says Oscar Horta, a philosopher and leading animal activist who recently helped direct a short film on how AI could affect wildlife.

Horta says he is concerned about the far-fetched videos of animals he has seen online lately, such as wild animals being rescued during fires and floods. He worries the likely AI-generated content will lead people to question legitimate rescue tactics and hamper fundraising efforts for them in the future. That’s not ideal, particularly at a time when extreme weather events are becoming more common.

Inauthentic content could also inspire people to act dangerously, harming animals in the process. “There are deepfakes of polar bears drowning and people on boats coming and rescuing them,” Horta says, calling the scenes “ridiculous” and “unrepresentative of what it means to help animals.”

Researchers have begun proposing ways to slow the creation and spread of AI-generated misinformation about animals. This month, Jeff Sebo, director of the Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy at New York University, began pushing AI developers to incorporate language into their model guidelines that would discourage them from generating responses potentially harmful to animals.

The idea is to “emphasize the importance of staying grounded in evidence and reason” when it comes to the possible suffering of individual creatures, while also avoiding being “overly preachy, overly moralizing, or refusing reasonable user requests,” Sebo says.

New laws in California and the EU now also require the most popular AI image generators to embed invisible tags signaling that content was made by artificial intelligence. Social media platforms then have to use those tags to publicly label AI-generated pictures and videos.

Greater public awareness about AI and increasing access to verification tools could further restore trust. Features in ChatGPT, Gemini, and Meta AI can identify whether an image was generated by the respective chatbot. But most people don’t have the time to upload every animal photo or video they see to the tools, and there are limitations, including caps on the number of images someone can check. Integrating verification tools directly into messaging apps and web browsers and turning them on by default (with privacy protections in place, of course) could make them much more useful.

Butler’s heartbreak may have been eased if her iPhone could have automatically warned that the first scammer’s picture of Brooklyn might be fake. About once a month, Butler says she gets another deepfake from someone else claiming to have found her cat. According to tests WIRED conducted, ChatGPT verified that it generated at least one of the images, which shows a purported Brooklyn eating in front of a doorstep. Using a 29-word prompt and the original photo of Brooklyn from the missing poster, WIRED was able to use ChatGPT to create a picture nearly identical to the scammer’s.

Butler can’t seem to escape from seeing AI-generated cat videos online. When one comes across her social media feeds, she blocks the user who posted it, but new accounts still keep showing up. She says she now spends more time in a Facebook group for artists who oppose AI with nearly 300,000 members. It’s become a new sanctuary, where she can enjoy art she reliably knows was created by humans as she awaits Brooklyn’s hopeful eventual return.

entries.title: Green Chef Meal Kit Review (2026): Great Ingredients, Layered Flavor
entries.summary: HelloFresh’s organic meal kit Green Chef offers transparent sourcing, layered cooking, and trustworthy gluten-free dishes.
entries.content:
HelloFresh’s organic-focused meal service offers fresh herbs and the best seafood I’ve had from a meal kit. The gluten-free options are also truly gluten-free.

Organic ingredients and independently validated gluten-free selections. Diverse food, sophisticated options, elegant simplicity in instructions.

TIRED

Prep times are a little longer than advertised. Will generate more dirty dishes than expected. Among the more expensive meal kits.

I am mean about fish. I grew up in the Pacific Northwest, where steelhead trout is an IYKYK religion, and I take it for granted that my salmon is better than your salmon. I all but gave up eating salmon while living on the East Coast, where acrid and mushy farm fish reigns.

And so it was a shock when HelloFresh’s organic meal delivery service, Green Chef, actually sent me wild-caught sockeye salmon. It was even more of a shock when I dug into the tender flesh of a (farmed) steelhead trout to discover it was flavorful, fatty, flaky, and subtle. These were, without question, the two best filets of fish that I've ever gotten from a meal kit, and I've tried and reviewed most every meal delivery service in existence.

Last year when I tested Green Chef’s meals, I focused on the meal kit's gluten-free options, for the simple reason that Green Chef is among the only meal delivery services to prepare its gluten-free meals in separate facilities—backed by a hearty validation from the Seattle-area Gluten Intolerance Group. More than half of Green Chef's meals are gluten-free as of August, mostly dishes like rice or quinoa that don't need gluten rather than pale imitations of gluteny things.

But on my most recent test of three meals and three market items this August, it was Green Chef's food sourcing overall that caught my attention—meticulous enough that I received a little apology note when my plum tomatoes weren't organic, a situation caused by an apparent shortfall of available organic Romas at the moment of shipping.

The proteins were flavorful. And even in August, the most difficult time to ship perishable food, my herbs and veggies had nary a wilted leaf—a difficult and rare achievement, especially for fresh herbs like the parsley in the gremolata for my Turkish-spiced steelhead trout.

At $14 a serving, Green Chef ranks among the more expensive meal kits (HelloFresh runs around $10–$12), and the 42-deep selection of meals doesn't match middle-of-the-market meal kits like HelloFresh and Marley Spoon, which each offer 100-plus. But the recipes are thoughtful, and the care taken with its ingredients—especially for those with eating restrictions—makes it one of the tastiest meal kit options I've tried, without requiring long cook times.

Here's my experience with Green Chef, and how it works.

Cost per meal

$14 per serving on most plans, plus $12 shipping per week

Meal plan options

Three to eight meals per week; sized for two, four, or six people

Lowest-cost plan at full price

$96 (including shipping), for three meals for two people

Size of weekly menu

More than 40 options, plus salad-kit, protein, and smoothie add-ons

Gluten-free meals?

More than half the menu is certified gluten-free

Plant-based meals?

About a third of dishes are vegetarian. The vegan selection is more limited.

Other dietary plans/restrictions

A third of meals are dairy-free. A third are listed as low-calorie or low added sugar. Five to 10 keto offerings a week. Produce and eggs are organic unless otherwise specified. Allergens are clearly marked.

Prep time

20 to 45 minutes

The Nuts and Bolts

Like many other meal delivery services, Green Chef is subscription-based. After selecting your diet preferences, whether Mediterranean or gluten-free, you'll be asked how many people you're serving and how many meals a week you'd like to receive. Cost is straightforward: It's $14 a meal, plus $12 shipping per week. Generally, for first-time customers, you'll get 50 percent off the first week.

Also, as with HelloFresh's other meal kits, you can choose which day of the week you want your meals delivered. On the appointed day, a well-organized green box will arrive with recipes and most of the ingredients you need to prepare the meals. The exceptions are basic staples like oil, butter, salt, and pepper. Each recipe comes clearly marked with allergens, whether sesame or tree nuts.

Packaging and insulation are relatively minimal and mostly paper-recyclable, with the exception of two ice packs and the individual plastic packaging housing some produce and meat. Even in an August heat wave, my ice packs remained mostly frozen, and my meat remained at food-safe temperatures.

Meat is stored up against the ice pack. Otherwise, each recipe is individually bagged in a paper bag, with recipe cards (and some other little marketing materials) on the top of the box, which means you won't have to sift around to find the proper ingredients. Most meals are advertised at around 30 minutes. Each will probably take you 10 minutes more than this to actually prep and cook.

Fair warning that Green Chef, like a lot of meal kits, makes liberal request of multiple mixing bowls for many recipes. A summer 2026 special deal offers two free Staub mixing bowls in addition to the usual trial discounts, making this a good time to sign up.

For gluten-free consumers, note that Green Chef is the first meal kit brand to be certified or validated as gluten-free by the Gluten Intolerance Group, one of few bodies that attempts to certify ingredients or restaurants as safe for the gluten-intolerant. In a conversation last year about the stringency of the validation process, GIG representative Christopher Lorenz told me his organization traces every ingredient used in Green Chef's meals, uses ISO-accredited in-person auditors, spot-checks and lab-tests delivery boxes for gluten, and also verifies that gluten-free meals are prepared in a dedicated facility.

Lorenz also checked for complaints and found that no one had filed a complaint that they'd been “glutened” by Green Chef during the years his organization had audited Green Chef's gluten-free meals.

Green Chef’s Food Is Mostly Organic, Delicious, and Varied

My testing last year showed that gluten-free meals from Green Chef were consistently among the most delicious I've tried from a meal kit claiming to offer gluten-free food—a low bar hurdled with aplomb. Rather than make pale imitations of gluteny things, Green Chef's meals were dishes that never needed wheat in the first place. This might include a kale and quinoa grilled chicken bowl with North African spice, steaks in red pepper sauce with green peas and rice, or a rice bowl topped with cabbage and honey ginger shrimp.

This year, gluten-free dishes included a lemon-oregano shrimp with schug and feta—a lemony-herbal romp served over rice livened up with dried apricots. (Adding dried fruit to liven up rice is a favored trick by Green Chef, one I might plan to add to my normal cooking routines.) The American-fished shrimp were plump and hearty, with no briny fishiness.

Yemeni schug remains one of my favorite condiments in existence, though this version could have been spicier. And the rice could have been more plentiful, perhaps. But these are small quibbles on a light, bright meal with lovely layers of flavor from herbal schug to toasted cauliflower and kale and the lightly tart bite of apricot.

I would almost never bring together this many ingredients on a weekday night, were they not helpfully bagged up in single portions. Indeed, if I tried, I probably would end up spending more at the grocery store than on the meal kit, as I discovered after an experiment last year.

But especially, I have been impressed with protein sourcing. A well-trimmed bavette steak last year came from a fourth-generation meat purveyor in Texas. So did my chicken breast this year, on a harissa chicken dish. Shrimp are Atlantic coast, not Southeast Asian coast. My salmon was wild-caught. My steelhead came from a fishery in Norway. Each is clearly and transparently marked—a rarity among proteins from meal delivery services.

That steelhead in particular was among my favorite home meals of the summer. The dish's secret, again, was layering: earthy spice on the fish, citric accents and crispness on the gremolata. The pleasing chew of dates countered the soft give of ginger-spiced couscous.

While eating it, I actually felt proud of myself—though it only took a scant 40 minutes to make. If anything, this summer's meals were more sophisticated, but lower effort, than the Green Chef meals I tried last year.

Quibbles

Green Chef's recipe cards are thoughtfully designed, with helpful pictures guiding the way. But their format tends to separate out each prep step in full, carrying the entire step through to completion, whether veggie chopping or couscous cooking.

This makes sense, of course. But this does lead to a simple caution: Green Chef does not hold your hand as well as some meal kits as regards the best order of operations. Read through each recipe in its entirety before cooking, and decide your game plan.

I found that I could get quite close to the recipe's allotted cook time only if I planned ahead and thought through my order of operations so that baking, sautéing, and pot-cooking can all happen more or less simultaneously. Otherwise, if you operate sequentially, you may end up discovering that a recipe takes twice as long as advertised.

Other little quibbles are that the standard quarter-cup serving of rice can feel skimpy compared to most Americans' eating habits. And you will often need more dishes than you expect, leading to a bit of cleanup after roasting pistachios with one pan while steaming couscous in another, with steelhead in the oven.

I did not regret any of this when eating a many-layered bowl full of healthily plump shrimp or a tender-flaky steelhead or wild-caught salmon. Sourcing good ingredients is more than half the work when it comes to cooking a delicious meal. Cleaning up an extra mixing bowl feels like a small price to pay.
